title: Three pricers, one price
objectives: Compare the three pricers and explain where they differ.
Tell noise from real differences with each pricer's error allowance.

screens.title: Where will they differ?

hints.text: Early exercise pays $K - S$ now. When is that most tempting?
Look at the deepest in-the-money strike.
More time means more interest on $K$ to earn by exercising: the one-year 120 put.

feedback.correct: The one-year 120 put: its American premium is £2.18.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The premium is largest deep in the money and with long to run.

byKey.r2c3: The at-the-money put has the most time value, but it is rarely worth exercising early. Its premium is 43p.

screens.prose: A difference means something only next to its noise. For the one-year 100 put, `mc_price` gives £5.9609 with standard error £0.0210; `bs_price` gives £5.9443.

The difference is £0.0166.

explain.text: A gap of 0.79 errors happens by chance about four times in ten. The dashboard reports each difference in pence and in errors. Model validation calls a European difference real only past about three.

screens.title: Worth exactly £20
screens.prose: The tree's American column has one round number: the three-month 120 put is worth £20.0000, exactly $K - S$. Its European price is £18.9467.
screens.question: Why is the American price exactly £20.00?

options.text: Exercising today beats holding
A put can never be worth more than $K - S$
options.why: A European put can exceed $K - S$ only when it is shallow; an American put is worth at least $K - S$. Here the two meet because the holder exercises now.

options.text: Rounding: the tree's price is close to £20 by chance
options.why: It is £20.0000 to four places, and exactly $K - S$ in the code: the max picked the exercise value at the root.

options.text: Black-Scholes is wrong for deep in-the-money puts
options.why: Black-Scholes is right for the European put, £18.95. The American right is worth more, and the tree sees it.

hints.text: At the root the tree takes $\max(\text{hold}, K - S)$.
Holding is worth less than £20, so the max picks exercise at once.

feedback.correct: The holder exercises at once: £20 now beats any wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the max at the root compares.

byKey.cap: The bound runs the other way for an American put: it is worth at least $K - S$.
byKey.round: It is exact: the max returned $K - S$ itself.
byKey.bs: Black-Scholes prices the European put correctly. The gap is the right to exercise.

explain.text: Deep in the money, receiving £120 now and investing it beats the small chance of more later. So the root is in the exercise region and the put is worth £20. This is where the premium, £1.05, is largest against the European price at three months.

screens.title: The comparison grid
screens.prose: Now the panel's table. `compare_grid` prices puts at every strike and expiry with your three pricers, one row per option, expiries outer and strikes inner. Every cell passes the same `seed` to `mc_price`, so neighbouring cells share their paths.

params.title: Expected (first rows)
lines: K     T      bs  tree_eu  tree_am_put      mc   mc_se

screens.question: Complete `compare_grid`.

widget.solution:
import pandas as pd

COLUMNS = ["K", "T", "bs", "tree_eu", "tree_am_put", "mc", "mc_se"]


def compare_grid(S, r, q, sigma, strikes, expiries, n_steps, n_paths, seed):
    """Puts priced three ways on a strike-by-expiry grid, one row per option.
    Every cell uses the same seed: common random numbers."""
    rows = []
    for T in expiries:
        for K in strikes:
            mc, se = mc_price(S, K, r, sigma, T, "put", n_paths, seed, True, q)
            rows.append({"K": K, "T": T,
                         "bs": bs_price(S, K, r, sigma, T, "put", q),
                         "tree_eu": crr_price(S, K, r, sigma, T, n_steps, "put", False, q),
                         "tree_am_put": crr_price(S, K, r, sigma, T, n_steps, "put", True, q),
                         "mc": mc, "mc_se": se})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=COLUMNS)

tests.call: [(float(k), float(t)) for k, t in zip(g['K'], g['T'])]

The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes 10 to 30 seconds.

The two tree columns are `crr_price(..., n_steps, "put", False, q)` and the same with `True`.
Append a dict with the seven keys, then build the frame with `columns=COLUMNS`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first failing test names the column that differs.

byKey.test-3: Your rows are in another order. Loop over expiries outside and strikes inside.
byKey.test-7: Your Monte Carlo column differs. Pass `seed` unchanged to every cell, with `antithetic=True`, `kind="put"` and `q`.

screens.title: What each price costs
screens.prose: The dashboard prices every quote on the chain, 130 of them. We timed one price of each kind in Pyodide: `bs_price` 3.7 µs, a 500-step American tree 50 ms, `mc_price` with 100,000 antithetic paths 18 ms. The 15-cell grid took 0.39 s.
screens.question: Which pricer costs most for the whole chain?

options.text: The American tree: about 6.5 s for 130 quotes
Monte Carlo, since it draws 100,000 random numbers per price
options.why: Random draws are cheap in NumPy: 18 ms a price, 2.3 s for the chain. The tree's 125,000 node updates cost more.

options.text: Black-Scholes, since it runs for every quote
options.why: Every pricer runs for every quote. At 3.7 µs, the whole chain costs half a millisecond.

hints.text: Multiply each time by 130.
The tree takes 50 ms a price.
$130 \times 50$ ms is 6.5 s; $130 \times 18$ ms is 2.3 s.

feedback.correct: The tree: 6.5 s, against 2.3 s for Monte Carlo and 0.5 ms for the formula.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale each per-price time to 130 quotes.

byKey.mc: Monte Carlo is the second most expensive here: 2.3 s for the chain.
byKey.bs: The formula is the cheapest by more than three orders of magnitude.

explain.text: The formula is about 5,000 times cheaper than Monte Carlo and 13,500 times cheaper than the tree, so the dashboard uses it wherever it is exact. The tree runs only where early exercise matters. Monte Carlo is a check here, and the pricer of last resort for exotic payoffs.

screens.title: Flagging the differences
screens.prose: The panel's last job is to say which differences matter. A Monte Carlo difference is noise within three errors; a tree difference within a penny. An American put above its European twin is real value; below it, a bug. `flag_differences` lists every difference beyond its allowance, with its reason.

params.title: Expected

screens.question: Complete `flag_differences`.

widget.starter:
import pandas as pd


def flag_differences(grid, tree_tol=0.01, n_se=3.0):
    """One row per difference beyond its noise allowance, with a reason.
    Checks per grid row, in this order:
      "mc":       |mc - bs| > n_se * mc_se          -> "pricer-error"
      "tree_eu":  |tree_eu - bs| > tree_tol          -> "pricer-error"
      "american": tree_am_put - tree_eu < -tree_tol  -> "pricer-error"
                  tree_am_put - tree_eu > tree_tol   -> "american-premium"
    diff is the signed difference (first minus second)."""
    out = []
    ...
    return pd.DataFrame(out, columns=["K", "T", "check", "diff", "reason"])
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on `hand_grid()`, six rows of the grid above (already defined). They use the clean grid, three planted bugs (a Monte Carlo price 5p off, an American put below its European one, a tree 3p off), a wider tolerance, and a grid with no premium. Flags are compared as tuples, `diff` rounded to 6 places. The first run loads pandas.

hints.text: Loop over `grid.to_dict("records")`: each row is a plain dict.
For each row run the three checks in order, appending a tuple when one fails.
`prem = g["tree_am_put"] - g["tree_eu"]`: below `-tree_tol` is a pricer error, above `tree_tol` a premium.

feedback.correct: Your flags catch all three planted bugs and label the premiums as real.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first failing test shows which planted bug your flags miss or mislabel.

byKey.test-1: On the clean grid only American premiums above a penny should appear, with reason `american-premium`.
byKey.test-2: The planted Monte Carlo price is 5p off with an error of 1.2p: beyond three errors, so `pricer-error`.
byKey.test-3: An American put 2p below its European one is a bug: `pricer-error`, not a premium.
byKey.test-7: With no premium and no bugs, return an empty frame that still has the five columns.

explain.text: The 5p Monte Carlo slip is 5.0 errors from Black-Scholes, so it is flagged. A premium is flagged too, but as value the panel explains rather than a fault. Keeping both in one table is what a validation report looks like.

screens.title: Two differences in one row
screens.prose: A reviewer reads one row of the grid, the one-year 110 put, and flags both differences as pricer errors.
screens.question: Which difference is a pricer error?

options.text: Neither: one is noise, one is value
Both: each pricer disagrees with the closed form
options.why: You compared every pricer with Black-Scholes as the truth. It is the truth only for the European put, and only within each pricer's noise.

options.text: The Monte Carlo one: 0.95p is a real gap
options.why: 0.95p against an error of 1.85p is 0.5 errors, well inside the noise.

options.text: The tree one: £1.05 is far beyond a penny
options.why: A penny is the allowance for the European tree. The American tree prices a different option, worth £1.05 more.

hints.text: Measure the MC gap in errors.
0.95p over 1.85p.
The tree row is American; Black-Scholes prices the European put.

feedback.correct: Neither is an error: one is noise, the other is value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each row, what the difference should be if both pricers are right.

byKey.both: Black-Scholes is a fair benchmark only for the European price, and only up to noise.
byKey.mc: Half an error happens by chance most of the time.
byKey.tree: The premium is real: the right to exercise early is worth £1.05 here.

explain.text: A Monte Carlo gap counts only in errors, and 0.5 is noise. An American price above the formula is the early-exercise premium, which no European formula can give. Flag a difference only after asking what both pricers should agree on.

screens.title: The noise allowances
screens.prose: Your panel's rules: $$|\text{mc} - \text{bs}| \le 3\,\text{SE},\qquad |\text{tree}_{\text{eu}} - \text{bs}| \le \text{tol},\qquad \text{tree}_{\text{am}} \ge \text{tree}_{\text{eu}} - \text{tol}.$$ Inside them, differences are noise. Beyond them, a difference is a bug, unless it is the American premium.
screens.question: A new pricer differs from Black-Scholes by 7p on a European call, with a standard error of 2p. What does the panel say?

options.text: A pricer error: 3.5 errors is too many
Noise: 7p is small against a £10 price
options.why: You judged the gap against the price. It must be judged against its error: 7p is 3.5 errors.

options.text: The American premium
options.why: The call is European, so there is no early exercise to explain the gap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gap by the error and compare with 3.

explain.text: $7/2 = 3.5$ errors, which chance gives about one time in 2,000. So the panel flags it as a pricer error. Re-run with more paths before you hunt the bug: a real error stays, noise shrinks.

screens.title: A validation team's first test
screens.prose: A model validation team checks a new pricer the same way: agree with the closed form where one exists, then explain every difference. They also ask where the simulation is weakest. Here are two three-month puts from the grid.
screens.question: What is the 80 put's standard error as a percentage of its price?

hints.text: Divide the error by the price.
That is about 4.1%.

feedback.correct: About 4.1%: ten times the at-the-money figure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the standard error by the Black-Scholes price for $K = 80$.

byKey.atm: That is the at-the-money put. Do the same for $K = 80$.
byKey.pence: That is the error in pence. Divide it by the price, 2.96p.

explain.text: Only about one path in 90 ends below £80, so the estimate rests on few payoffs. The error is small in pence but 4.1% of the price, and wing vols are sensitive to it. The dashboard's pricer panel shows these errors beside every price, as the trade ticket did.

ideas: On European puts the three pricers agree: the 500-step tree within 0.4p and Monte Carlo within 1.3 standard errors of Black-Scholes on every cell of the grid.
The American put differs by the early-exercise premium, real value from 0.03p to £2.18 on our grid, which no European formula can give.
`flag_differences` judges each gap against its allowance: three errors for Monte Carlo, a penny for the tree, and American at least European.

quiz.prose: A colleague reads the expiry column of the grid as `grid.T`.
quiz.question: What do they get?

options.text: The transposed frame
The `T` column
options.why: Attribute access usually returns a column, but `.T` is pandas' transpose and wins.

options.text: An `AttributeError`
options.why: No error is raised, which is why the slip is easy to miss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `.T` has a meaning of its own on every DataFrame.

explain.text: `DataFrame.T` transposes the frame, so the expiries never appear. Bracket access, `grid["T"]`, is safe for any column name.
